messages.author: b03a46e3cd9641a4
messages.subject: novice question
parts:
Greetings all,
I will be performing spotlight counts of white-tailed deer using distance
sampling. In my lit. search so far, I have not seen mention of methods for
using distance sampling on serpentine 'transects' (I will use a vehicle on
mountain roads). I have only seen methods for straight transects. I am
looking for references that address this question.
TIA,
CL

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: novice question
parts:
> > I will be performing spotlight counts of white-tailed deer using distance
> > sampling. In my lit. search so far, I have not seen mention of methods for
> > using distance sampling on serpentine 'transects' (I will use a vehicle on
> > mountain roads). I have only seen methods for straight transects. I am
> > looking for references that address this question.

There is a good reason for this ... we strongly discourage use of roads
for transects! It is rare for animal density along roads to be
representative of overall density - and rarer still to be able to
demonstrate that this is so. Further, you can't even assume that road
transects will give you a useful relative measure of abundance, as traffic
may increase over time, or hunter activity vary with time, leading to
varying densities along roads that do not reflect variation in the wider
population.

However, if you plan to do it anyway, you should look at

Quang, P. X. and Becker, E. F. (1999) Aerial survey sampling of contour
transects using double-count and covariate data, in \em Marine Mammal
Survey and Assessment Methods\em (eds G. W. Garner, S. C. Amstrup,
J. L. Laake, B. F. J. Manly, L. L. McDonald and D. G. Robertson), Balkema,
Rotterdam, pp. 87--97.

The issues addressed by Quang and Becker for contour transects will apply
also to road transects.

Lex Hiby has also looked at the issue of curved transects - in his case,
they are transects through rain forest, where existing paths are used. I
don't think his work is published yet.

You should also look at the following paper:

Gill, R. M. A., Thomas, M. L. and Stocker, D. (1997) The use of portable
thermal imaging for estimating deer population density in forest
habitats. Journal of Applied Ecology, 34, 1273--86.


Steve Buckland

messages.author: e01f486fac57c93c
messages.subject: Re: novice question
parts:
While studying chameleons in Madagascar we have attempted to compare curved
transects (ie. set along trails) and straight (i.e. non-trail) transects.
Some preliminary data is published in Oryx:

Jenkins, R. K. B., Brady, L. D., Huston, K., Kauffmann, J. L. D.,
Rabearivony, J., Raveloson, G. and Rowcliffe, J. M. (1999) The population
status of chameleons within Ranomafana National Park, Madagascar and
recommendations for future monitoring. Oryx, 33, 38-46.

To summarise, we found that densities of species were different between the
two transects - usually higher along trails. There are many possible reasons
for this, but ultimately we concur with the general view that trails are
best avoided.

---------------------------------

messages.author: eacc985cd7d1a89f
messages.subject: Re: novice question
parts:
We have been using distance sampling to estimate deer density in a number of forest areas using thermal imaging. There are several comments I can make about the problem of using roads:

We usually only work from small forest roads that are not open to the public.
There appears to be much more avoidance from public roads (though I havent yet tested them for significance)

We have been using thermal imaging because it can detect deer at greater distances, even if partly hidden in vegetation, and doesn't cast a beam which the deer can see. Even so, we have still had problems with avoidance in some instances. In most cases it seems to be avoidance of the observer (not the road) because results have often been better on subsequent occasions once the importance of minimising disturbance is made clear to the observer. This can be done minimising speed and by focussing on the road ahead, (rather than at right angles into the forest), because deer close to the road sometimes walk away when they hear a vehicle coming.

We tried alternatives to forest roads - one was to try cutting paralell transects from a random starting point and walking these, but the we found (apart from the additional cost) that visibility was much more restricted from a narrow path than from a road, so we have not tried these again. Attempts to walk through the forest off paths always created more disturbance than from a road, so were worse.

Another concern with roads is that they may not penetrate all habitats within the area - this is more likely in mountainous terrain. Further, the terrain itself affects visibility, because animals are more easily detected on opposing valley slopes than on the observer's slope.

In summary, using roads can give good results, but only with care and under certain circumstances. It would clearly be preferable to avoid them altogether, but that may be completely impractical. Any methods that can be devised to control for the various limitations and biases involved would clearly be very useful. I would have thought that GIS would be a useful tool to support the design and analysis of surveys (and could provide covariates) but I'm not aware of any attempts yet to combine them with distance sampling. Any ideas or suggestions would be welcome!


Robin Gill
Forest Research
Alich Holt Lodge
Wrecclesham
Surrey GU10 4LH
01420 22255
